L169: # Posterior vitreous detachment
L170: 
L171: Posterior vitreous detachment (PVD) is a condition where your vitreous gel comes away from the retina at the back of your eye.
L172: ## On this page
L173: 
L174:   * 【69†What causes PVD?】
L175:   * 【70†What are the symptoms of PVD?】
L176:   * 【71†How do I cope with my floaters?】
L177:   * 【72†Is there any treatment for PVD?】
L178:   * 【73†Are there any complications of a PVD?】
L179:   * 【74†What activities can I carry on doing if I have PVD?】
L180:   * 【75†Further information and support】
L181: This detachment is caused by changes in your vitreous gel. PVD isn’t painful and it doesn’t cause sight loss, but you may have symptoms such as seeing floaters (small, dark spots or shapes) and flashing lights.
L182: 
L183: These symptoms will calm down as your brain learns to ignore them. With time, you should be able to see just as well as you could before your PVD started.
L184: The symptoms of PVD are very similar to those of a different eye condition called 【76†retinal detachment】, which needs prompt treatment to stop you losing part or all of the sight in your eye. Because of this, it’s important to have your eyes examined by an ophthalmologist (hospital eye doctor) or an optometrist (also known as an optician) within 24 hours of noticing any symptoms so that an accurate diagnosis can be made. You can do this by visiting your optometrist or attending A&E or eye casualty.
L185: You can also call 111 for advice about where to go to get your eyes checked.
L186: About 10 to 15 per cent of people with PVD develop a retinal tear, which, if left untreated can develop into a retinal detachment. A retinal tear or detachment can be successfully treated if diagnosed early.
L187: 
L188: Most people diagnosed with PVD will not develop a retinal tear or detachment.
L189: 
L190: This page contains a summary of our information on PVD. To read our full information, download our Understanding posterior vitreous detachment booklet, which is accredited by the Royal College of Ophthalmologists:

L198: ## What causes PVD?
L199: 
L200: 【79†Your eye】 is filled with a clear gel called the vitreous. The vitreous helps to keep your eye’s shape. It is made up mainly of water and a protein called collagen.
L201: As you age, it is common for the vitreous to become more watery and less like a gel. When the vitreous gets too soft, it loses its shape, and comes away from the retina and shrinks in towards the centre of your eye. Once the vitreous detaches, it does not reattach again. This is not a problem as we don’t need the vitreous attached to the retina to see well. PVD is a natural change in the eye and is not a sign of another eye health problem.
L202: The most common cause of PVD is age. Most people with PVD are over the age of 50 but you can have a PVD in your 40s, particularly if you’re short-sighted or if your eye has been injured or you’ve had previous eye surgery.
L203: 
L204: It’s normal to get PVD in both eyes, although often it will occur in one eye at a time. Usually people get PVD in their other eye between six months to a couple of years after the first eye. As PVD is a natural change, there is no way to prevent a PVD from happening.
L205: ## What are the symptoms of PVD?
L206: 
L207: PVD can cause several symptoms:
L208: 
L209:   * Floaters for the first time or more floaters than you had before. The new floaters are usually noticed suddenly. There may be lots of new floaters or commonly a large cobweb-like floater.
L210:   * Flashes of light in your vision, usually like brief streaks of light in your peripheral (side) vision.
L211:   * Blurred vision.
L212: As the process of a PVD can last some weeks to some months, your symptoms may be ongoing for this period. Generally, your floaters and the flashes of light will gradually calm down and become less obvious to you. You might be aware of your floaters in the long-term following a PVD, although they are generally not as noticeable as when they first began. As long as the symptoms are not worsening after your eyes have been checked and PVD is diagnosed, then they are not usually a cause for concern.
L213: If you’re worried about any symptoms that don’t go away, speak to your optometrist or ophthalmologist about it.
L214: ### Floaters
L215: 
L216: Floaters are very common and many people have them, even if they don’t have PVD. They’re floating clumps of cells that form in your vitreous. You can see them because they cast shadows on your retina when light comes into your eye. These floaters do not harm your eye.
L217: Floaters can be different shapes and sizes – dots that can look like flies, threads, circles, clouds, spiders or cobwebs. You may notice that your floaters move around a lot, or they may not seem to move much at all. They tend to be more obvious on a sunny day or when looking at a bright computer screen or a white or lightly coloured background.
L218: You may only have a few floaters or you may have many of them. Floaters may appear quite suddenly, and they may be very frustrating or worrying to you. When they’re at their most intense, you might think that your floaters will always interfere with your vision, but for most people, they become less obvious over time. Floaters never leave the eye but become less noticeable as the vitreous settles down and your brain learns to ignore them.
L219: ### Flashes of light
L220: 
L221: When your vitreous pulls away from your retina, your retina reacts to this stimulation by sending a signal to your brain. Your brain processes this signal as a small, short flash of light. You’ll often see more in dark or dim lighting as they will show up more against a darker background. These flashes of light won’t affect you for as long as floaters, and they will probably become a lot less frequent once the vitreous has fully come away from your retina.
L222: ## How do I cope with my floaters?
L223: 
L224: If you have a large floater, moving your eyes gently round in circles may help. This moves the vitreous inside your eyes and can sometimes move the floater out of your direct line of vision so you’re less aware of it.

L13: # Floaters and flashes in the eyes
L14: 
L15: Dots and lines (floaters) or flashes of light in your vision are common. They're not usually serious.
L16: ## Symptoms of floaters and flashes
L17: 
L18: Floaters in your vision can look like:
L19: 
L20:   * small dark dots
L21:   * squiggly lines
L22:   * rings
L23:   * cobwebs
L24: 
L25: Flashes look like sudden flashes of light.
L26: 
L27: They're usually harmless and not a sign of anything serious, especially if:
L28: 
L29:   * you've had them for a long time
L30:   * they're not getting worse
L31:   * your vision is not affected
L32: 
L33: Flashes may eventually stop, and floaters often become less noticeable as you get used to them.
L34: ## Urgent advice: Ask for an urgent opticians appointment or get help from NHS 111 if:
L35: 
L36:   * you have floaters or flashes in your vision for the first time
L37:   * you suddenly get floaters or flashes in your vision
L38:   * the number of floaters or flashes suddenly increases
L39:   * you have a dark "curtain" or shadow moving across your vision
L40:   * you also have blurred vision
L41:   * you also have eye pain
L42:   * floaters start after eye surgery or an eye injury
L43: These could be signs of a serious problem with the back of your eye, which could permanently affect your vision if it's not treated quickly.
L44: 
L45: You can call 111 or 【6†get help from 111 online†111.nhs.uk】.
L46: ## What happens at your appointment
L47: 
L48: If you have problems with floaters or flashes in your vision your eyes will be checked at an opticians to see if you need to be seen by an eye doctor (ophthalmologist) for more tests or treatment.
L49: 
L50: You'll usually only need treatment if you have a problem that could affect your vision.
L51: ## Causes of floaters and flashes
L52: 
L53: Lots of people, particularly older people, get floaters and flashes.
L54: 
L55: They're usually caused by a harmless process called posterior vitreous detachment (PVD), where the gel inside your eyes changes.
L56: 
L57: Sometimes they can be caused by 【7†retinal detachment】.
L58: 
L59: This is serious and can lead to permanent vision loss if not treated.
L60: 
L61: Floaters and flashes can also happen for no obvious reason.
L62:

L285: # Posterior vitreous detachment
L286: 
L287: ## Patient information A-Z
L288: 
L289: [Button: Print this page]
L290: ## Your eye
L291: 
L292: The back of the eye is filled with a jelly-like substance called vitreous. This is normally transparent.
L293: 
L294: 【92†Image: illustration of the eye showing the position vitreous in relation to retina, iris, pupil, lens and optic nerve†media.cuh.nhs.uk】
L295: 
L296: Illustration of the eye showing the position of the vitreous in relation to retina, iris, pupil, lens and optic nerve
L297: A natural ageing process causes the lining of the vitreous to separate from the retina. When this occurs it is usually quite sudden causing ‘floaters’ to appear in the vision and sometimes an associated ‘arc’ of flashing light at the side of the vision. The light may be quite dim so that it is seen most easily at dusk or in the dark.
L298: 
L299: When the vitreous has separated from the retina it is known as a posterior vitreous detachment.
L300: 
L301: Will it affect my vision?
L302: The floaters can be annoying but they are harmless. They usually persist but become less noticeable with time.
L303: 
L304: The flashing light will usually subside over weeks, but may sometimes last several months.
L305: 
L306: What treatment will be needed?
L307: 
L308: No treatment is needed for a posterior vitreous detachment.
L309: 
L310: What complications could occur?
L311: 
L312: Occasionally as the vitreous separates it can tear the retina. This may cause some bleeding (vitreous haemorrhage) within the eye, or even a retinal detachment.
L313: This complication is more likely in short sighted people. The ophthalmologist who examined you will have ensured that there is no retinal tear or retinal detachment present at the moment.
L314: 
L315: What symptoms need to be reported?
L316: 
L317:   * Shower of dot-like floaters
L318:   * Loss of vision
L319:   * Growing dark shadow from the edge of the vision
L320: 
L321: If you experience any of these symptoms please contact us immediately:
L322: 
L323:   * Emergency Eye Clinic - 01223 217778
L324:   * Vitreo Retinal Nurses - 01223 274865
L325: Retinal detachment and vitreous haemorrhage (bleeding into the vitreous) are potentially blinding conditions. However timely treatment and surgery is effective in most cases.
L326: 
L327: For further information on retinal detachment please 【93†visit the Vitreoretinal Service website (opens in a new tab)†www.vitreoretinalservice.org】.
